title: Processes and Signals
oneLiner: See what's running, run things in the background, and stop what's stuck.
keyTakeaway: Every running program is a process with a PID. ps and top show them; & runs a command in the background; kill PID asks a process to stop (SIGTERM), and kill -9 forces it (SIGKILL) when it won't. nice and renice set how politely a process shares the CPU.
explanation:
A process is a running program: your shell (the program that reads and runs the commands you type), the sleep you start, the web server on a real box. Each has a process ID (PID), an owner, and a parent that started it. ps lists processes (ps aux on most full Linux systems; plain ps here), and top shows a live view sorted by CPU use -- press q to leave it. Combine ps with grep to find one by name.

Normally the shell waits for a command to finish. Put & on the end and it runs in the background instead, giving you your prompt back; jobs lists your background jobs, fg brings one back to the front, and Ctrl+C stops whatever is in the front. $! holds the PID of the last background job.

kill doesn't necessarily kill: it sends a signal. The default, SIGTERM, asks the process to shut down cleanly -- finish writing files, close connections. Well-behaved programs (and container platforms like Kubernetes) rely on that. kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which the process can't catch or ignore; use it when SIGTERM didn't work, knowing the program gets no chance to clean up. killall name signals every process with that name.

Priority is set by a nice value from -20 (greediest) to 19 (most polite); normal is 0. nice -n 10 command starts something politely, and renice 10 -p PID sets a running one's value (BusyBox's renice -n 10 adds 10 to the current value instead). Ordinary users can make their processes nicer but only root can make them greedier.
